title: Does exercise reduce symptoms of depression?
claimTopic: Whether regular exercise reduces symptoms of depression.

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether supervised aerobic exercise reduces symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder.
study.participants: 90 adults ages 25 to 60 with major depressive disorder, diagnosed by a clinician, were recruited from two outpatient clinics in a large US city. None were taking medication for depression. All gave written informed consent and were told they could leave the study at any time.
study.method: Participants were randomly assigned to 12 weeks of supervised aerobic exercise (brisk walking or cycling, 40 minutes, three times a week) or 12 weeks of supervised stretching for the same amount of time. Depression was measured before and after with a 21-item symptom questionnaire (0 to 63; higher scores mean more severe symptoms) given by an interviewer who did not know each person's group.
study.results: Mean scores fell from 29 to 17 in the aerobic exercise group and from 29 to 24 in the stretching group. The difference between the groups after 12 weeks was statistically significant.
study.discussion: Aerobic exercise reduced symptoms more than stretching, which gave the same time and attention without aerobic activity.

plot.label: Grouped bar graph of mean depression scores before and after 12 weeks: aerobic exercise 29 then 17, stretching 29 then 24 (invented data for practice)

study.introduction: Researchers compared exercise with two established treatments for depression in older adults.
study.participants: 120 adults ages 50 to 75 with major depressive disorder were recruited from community health centers in three US states. All gave informed consent, and a university institutional review board approved the study.
study.method: Participants were randomly assigned to 16 weeks of group aerobic exercise (three sessions a week), weekly cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), or an SSRI antidepressant. Depression was measured before and after with the same 21-item questionnaire (0 to 63).
study.results: Mean scores fell by 12 points with exercise, 13 points with CBT and 12 points with the antidepressant. The differences among the three groups were not statistically significant.
study.discussion: For these older adults, exercise reduced symptoms about as much as CBT or medication. The study had no untreated group.

table.caption: Mean depression scores (0 to 63) before and after 16 weeks (invented data for practice)

sources.title: Physical activity and mood in teenagers

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether teenagers who are more physically active report fewer symptoms of depression.
study.participants: 2,000 students ages 14 to 18 at 20 public high schools in Canada completed an online survey. Parents gave consent and students gave assent; answers were anonymous.
study.method: Students reported how many hours a week they spent in physical activity and completed a 10-item depression symptom checklist (0 to 30; higher scores mean more symptoms). The researchers did not assign activity levels.
study.results: Students who reported 5 or more hours of activity a week had a mean symptom score of 9, compared with 11 for 2 to 4 hours and 14 for 0 to 1 hour. More activity was associated with fewer symptoms.
study.discussion: Active teenagers reported fewer symptoms, but because activity was not manipulated, the study cannot show that activity caused the difference.

plot.label: Bar graph of mean depression symptom score by weekly hours of physical activity: 0 to 1 hours 14, 2 to 4 hours 11, 5 or more hours 9 (invented data for practice)

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.

rubric.point: Proposes a defensible claim that answers whether regular exercise reduces symptoms of depression.
accept: Regular exercise reduces symptoms of depression.
Aerobic exercise can reduce depressive symptoms about as well as therapy or medication.
Exercise reduces symptoms of depression for adults with major depressive disorder.

parts.sample: Regular aerobic exercise reduces symptoms of depression, and for adults with major depressive disorder it can work about as well as CBT or antidepressant medication.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Cites one source and states a specific, accurate result from it that supports the claim (not a method or participant detail).
accept: In Source 1, scores fell from 29 to 17 with aerobic exercise but only from 29 to 24 with stretching.
According to Source 2, exercise lowered scores by 12 points, about the same as CBT (13) and medication (12).

parts.sample: According to Source 1, adults with major depressive disorder who did aerobic exercise for 12 weeks saw their mean depression score fall from 29 to 17, while those who only stretched fell from 29 to 24, a statistically significant difference.

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: Because the stretching group got the same time and attention, the extra drop in the exercise group points to the aerobic activity itself.

rubric.point: Applies a psychological concept (not a restricted term) to the evidence and links it to the claim.
accept: endorphins and other neurotransmitters released during aerobic activity (biological perspective)
self-efficacy built by meeting exercise goals
positive reinforcement from activities that bring mood rewards

parts.sample: Both groups spent the same time with supervisors, so the extra improvement in Source 1 comes from the aerobic activity itself. This fits the biological perspective: aerobic exercise increases the release of endorphins and changes the activity of other neurotransmitters linked to mood, which would lower symptoms. Because the aerobic group improved more than the stretching group, this suggests exercise reduces symptoms of depression.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Cites a different source from B(i) and states a specific, accurate result that supports the claim.
accept: In Source 2, exercise lowered scores by 12 points, close to CBT's 13 and medication's 12, with no significant difference.
Source 3 found teens with 5 or more hours of activity had a mean score of 9, compared with 14 for 0 to 1 hour.

parts.sample: In Source 2, older adults with major depressive disorder who did 16 weeks of group aerobic exercise improved by 12 points, about the same as those who had CBT (13 points) or took an SSRI (12 points); the differences were not statistically significant.

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding from the one in B(ii).

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: Exercise matched two established treatments, so it is a real alternative.

rubric.point: Applies a different psychological concept from B(ii) and links it to the evidence and the claim.
accept: evidence-based practice: exercise matched treatments already supported by research
the biopsychosocial model: group exercise adds social support

parts.sample: Source 2 shows exercise reducing symptoms as much as CBT and medication, two treatments that already have strong research support. In evidence-based practice, clinicians choose treatments using the best research together with the client's preferences, so this result means exercise can be offered as an effective option, especially to people who prefer not to take medication. This supports the claim that exercise reduces symptoms of depression.
